question: Which aeroplanes are single-engine Class B?

options.text: Any aeroplane certified in the aerobatic category, whatever its engine

explanation: Class B aeroplanes are propeller-driven, with a maximum approved passenger seating of 9 or less and a maximum take-off mass of 5 700 kg or less.

question: Which categories does the small aeroplane certification code cover?
explanation: The small aeroplane code contains requirements for normal, utility and aerobatic category aeroplanes, and for commuter category aeroplanes.

question: Under the basic rules for commercial transport, when may a single-engine Class B aeroplane fly at night?
explanation: One of the general requirements is that a single-engine Class B aeroplane is not operated at night in commercial air transport.

question: Under the basic rules, in which conditions may a single-engine Class B aeroplane be flown in IMC?

options.text: Whenever an instrument rating is held

explanation: It must not be operated in instrument meteorological conditions except under special VFR.

question: Why must a single-engine Class B aeroplane not fly above a cloud layer that extends below the minimum safe altitude?

options.text: The aeroplane could not climb above the cloud tops safely
The pilot could not see where to land
The engine could ice up in cloud

explanation: If the engine failed, the pilot would have to descend through cloud without seeing the ground and could not make a safe forced landing.

question: What must be available en route for a single-engine Class B aeroplane?

options.text: An alternate aerodrome within every 30 minutes of flying time
Surfaces for a safe forced landing

explanation: The aeroplane must not be operated unless surfaces are available along the route on which a safe forced landing can be made after an engine failure.

question: For a Class B aeroplane, where does the gross take-off distance end?

options.text: At a screen height of 35 ft
At a screen height of 50 ft

explanation: The gross take-off distance runs from the start of the take-off to 50 ft above the take-off surface, with take-off power set and the specified speed reached at the screen.

question: For a single-engine Class B aeroplane, what is the minimum rotation speed VR?
explanation: For a single-engine aeroplane, VR must not be less than VS1, the stall speed in the take-off configuration.

question: For a single-engine Class B aeroplane, what is the minimum speed at the 50 ft screen?

options.text: The higher of a safe speed and 1.2 VS1
The greater of 1.1 VMC and 1.2 VS1, plus a 5 kt margin

explanation: The take-off safety speed at 50 ft must be at least the greater of a speed that is safe under all reasonably expected conditions and 1.2 VS1.

question: How many take-off requirements apply to a single-engine Class B aeroplane?

options.text: Two: field length and climb gradient
Three: field length, climb and obstacles

explanation: The only take-off requirement is that the take-off can be completed within the available distances, the field length requirement.

question: With no stopway or clearway, what is the field length requirement for a Class B take-off?

options.text: Gross TOD × 1.15 must not exceed TORA
Gross TOD × 1.25 must not exceed TORA
Gross TOD must not exceed TORA
Gross TOD × 1.3 must not exceed TORA

explanation: With no stopway or clearway, the gross take-off distance multiplied by 1.25 must not exceed the TORA.

question: With a stopway and/or clearway, which three conditions apply to the gross take-off distance?

options.text: TOD ≤ TORA, TOD × 1.3 ≤ ASDA, TOD × 1.15 ≤ TODA
TOD ≤ TORA, TOD × 1.15 ≤ ASDA, TOD × 1.3 ≤ TODA
TOD × 1.25 ≤ TORA, TOD × 1.3 ≤ TODA, TOD × 1.15 ≤ ASDA

explanation: With stopway or clearway: TOD must not exceed TORA, TOD × 1.3 must not exceed ASDA, and TOD × 1.15 must not exceed TODA.

question: The gross take-off distance is 3 000 ft and there is no stopway or clearway. What is the minimum TORA?
explanation: 3 000 × 1.25 = 3 750 ft. 1.15 and 1.3 are the factors for TODA and ASDA.

question: With no stopway or clearway, how much runway should remain when a Class B aeroplane reaches the screen height?

options.text: None; it may reach the screen right at the end of the TORA

explanation: TOD × 1.25 ≤ TORA means the TOD is at most 80% of the TORA, so at least 20% of the runway is left (a 25% safety margin on the gross distance).

question: The TORA is 3 200 ft and there is no stopway or clearway. What is the greatest gross take-off distance allowed?
explanation: TOD × 1.25 ≤ 3 200, so TOD ≤ 3 200 ÷ 1.25 = 2 560 ft. Dividing by 1.15 gives 2 783 ft.

question: TORA 3 000 ft, ASDA 3 600 ft, TODA 3 300 ft. What is the greatest gross take-off distance allowed?
explanation: Limits: TORA 3 000; ASDA ÷ 1.3 = 2 769; TODA ÷ 1.15 = 2 870. The lowest, about 2 770 ft, is the limit set by the ASDA.

question: TORA 3 000 ft, ASDA 3 500 ft, TODA 3 400 ft. The gross TOD is 2 800 ft. Which requirement is NOT met?
What is the difference between the gross and net take-off distance of a Class B aeroplane?

options.text: The net one includes the factor
The net distance excludes the airborne part of the take-off
The gross distance includes the factor

explanation: The gross distance is the expected (average) performance; multiplying by the factor (e.g. 1.25) gives the net distance, the worst case expected.

question: Which of these must be accounted for in the gross take-off distance?
explanation: The gross TOD must account for mass, pressure altitude, ambient temperature, runway surface type and condition, runway slope, and factored wind.

question: What wind must be used in the Class B take-off calculation?

options.text: No more than 150% of the headwind
The full headwind and the full tailwind as reported by the tower

explanation: As for all classes, the gross TOD must use not more than 50% of the reported headwind and not less than 150% of the reported tailwind.

question: What factor is applied to the take-off distance for dry grass (up to 20 cm, firm soil)?
explanation: Dry grass increases the take-off distance by 20% (factor 1.2); wet grass by 30% (factor 1.3).

question: What factor is applied to the take-off distance for wet grass?
explanation: Wet grass on firm soil (up to 20 cm long) uses a factor of 1.3.

question: What factor is applied to the take-off distance for a wet paved runway?
explanation: For a wet paved runway the factor is 1.0, so no increase is required for the take-off distance.

question: What correction is applied for runway slope in the Class B take-off calculation?
explanation: The take-off distance is increased by 5% (factor 1.05) for each 1% upslope. No reduction is allowed for downslope, which adds a safety margin.

question: Why is no allowance made for a downslope in the take-off calculation?

options.text: A downslope always increases the distance
Ignoring it adds a safety margin

explanation: A downslope would shorten the take-off distance, so ignoring it keeps an extra margin.

question: The gross TOD on a paved dry level runway is 2 400 ft. What is it on dry grass with a 2% upslope?
explanation: 2 400 × 1.2 (dry grass) × 1.10 (2% upslope) = 3 168 ft. Leaving out the slope gives 2 880 ft.

question: The corrected gross TOD is 3 168 ft and there is no stopway or clearway. What is the minimum TORA?
A take-off chart gives 2 200 ft on a paved dry runway. The runway is wet grass with a 1% upslope. What is the corrected gross distance?
explanation: 2 200 × 1.3 × 1.05 = 3 003 ft, about 3 000 ft. Leaving out the slope gives 2 860 ft.

question: On a Class B take-off distance graph, what does the first (left) carpet account for?
explanation: The left carpet combines temperature and pressure altitude, which together account for air density.

question: On a typical Class B take-off graph, why do the headwind and tailwind lines have different slopes?

options.text: The wind factors are built in
Headwinds always increase the take-off distance on grass

explanation: The different slopes show the regulatory wind factors have already been applied, so the reported wind is entered directly.

question: What does the last carpet of a Class B take-off graph (labelled "obstacle height") represent?

options.text: A real obstacle located beyond the end of the runway

explanation: The take-off is not complete until 50 ft, so the last carpet adds the airborne distance from lift-off to the 50 ft screen.

question: Why must the pilot fly the VR and screen speeds shown on the take-off graph?

options.text: They are the minimum control speeds
The graph was constructed using those speeds
They give the best glide in an engine failure
They are required by air traffic control

explanation: The chart's distances assume those speeds; flying different ones means the chart performance will not be achieved.
